title: Global Potential of Agrivoltaics: Agriculture‐First and Radiation‐Limited Analysis
content:
Abstract

With rising global food and energy demand, agrivoltaics offer a viable solution for co-producing crops and solar electricity on shared land. Despite extensive field-scale design and optimization studies, a large-scale, crop-specific assessment constrained by light availability is still missing. Here, we introduce a radiation-limited framework that uses growing-season daily light integral (DLI) to set minimum light budgets for wheat, maize, rice, and soybean, and the agrivoltaics light utilization ratio (ALUR) metric to quantify the surplus light available for photovoltaic (PV) electricity generation. This enables a global first-order assessment of light availability revealing regional potentials and constraints to agrivoltaic adoption. Four agrivoltaic scenarios were explored by varying the light reserved for the crop: (a) literature-based crop light targets (SCT,crop), (b) empirical reference values representing the growing-season light received across the global distribution of each crop (SCR,crop), (c) a low reserve favoring electricity generation (SC20; 20 mol m−2 day−1), and (d) a conservative reserve favoring food security (SC40; 40 mol m−2 day−1). Even under the conservative scenario SC40, the total estimated mean global electricity-generation potential is 109 PWh yr−1 (95% uncertainty interval: 39–190 PWh yr−1). The estimated radiation-based potential is sensitive to the crop-specific DLI allocation, particularly in India and China, but remains substantial across the United States, Brazil, Argentina, Iran, and Pakistan. These findings suggest that while agrivoltaics are not a “one-size-fits-all” solution, their strategic application can mitigate the land-use conflict between energy and food production.
